item.title: More about «Neutrality Initiative»
item.description:
Published on 3 July 2026

On 27 September 2026 the Swiss electorate will vote on the Neutrality Initiative. The central question is whether we wish to retain neutrality in its current form, or whether an article should be inserted into the Federal Constitution requiring a stricter practice of neutrality. The latter would mark a clear change of direction. Neutrality has been enshrined in the Federal Constitution since 1848. The outcome of the vote does not call Switzerland’s neutrality into question. The point is how it should be applied in future.

Switzerland’s neutrality has been enshrined in the Federal Constitution since 1848. It is internationally recognised and safeguarded under international law. Switzerland uses its neutrality to protect its security, independence and prosperity. Neutrality contributes to Switzerland’s ability to provide its good offices.

Aim of the Neutrality Initiative

The initiative calls for the stricter practice of neutrality and seeks to add a new article to the Federal Constitution stating that:

  • Switzerland’s neutrality shall be perpetual and armed;
  • Switzerland shall not join any military or defence alliance, neither shall it cooperate with such an alliance, unless Switzerland is under military attack or such an attack is being prepared;
  • Switzerland shall not take part in armed conflicts between third countries and shall not impose sanctions against warring parties. Exceptions are made for sanctions decided by the United Nations (UN) and measures to prevent the circumvention of sanctions; and
  • Switzerland uses its neutrality to fulfil its role as mediator.

neutralitaet-ja.ch

Position of the Federal Council and Parliament

The Federal Council and Parliament reject the Neutrality Initiative without offering a counter-proposal. In their essence, the demands of the initiative correspond to the legal obligations of a neutral state, which Switzerland already upholds in practice.

  • Switzerland is permanently neutral, therefore its neutrality is already perpetual.
  • It is current practice that, as a permanently neutral state, Switzerland does not join any military or defence alliance such as NATO.
  • Under the present system Switzerland does not take part in armed conflicts between third countries.
  • Switzerland already adopts all UN sanctions. As a member of the UN it is required to do so.
  • The initiative committee is calling for Switzerland to use its neutrality in its role as mediator and to promote peace. That is already the current practice.

Where the demands of the initiative exceed what is the practice today, they damage Switzerland's interests:

  • Compared with current practice the initiative would curtail the flexibility that allows Switzerland to protect its security, independence and prosperity. This room for manoeuvre is particularly important amid a deteriorating security situation.
  • The initiative would impede cooperation on security policy. Switzerland cannot wait until it is attacked to begin cooperating, as the initiative envisages, as this would have grave consequences for the country's security. Switzerland would be excluded from knowledge-sharing, cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy, and be less secure in the event of an attack.
  • Sanctions are a means of responding to violations of international law and threats to the international order. As a small state, Switzerland benefits especially from this order. Under the initiative Switzerland would no longer be able to adopt sanctions against warring states, which would impact on both it’s interests and reputation. In certain cases it might also trigger a backlash from other states.

Neutrality Initiative: without counter-proposal, the Federal Council recommends rejection (Federal Council press release, 26.6.2024)

Dispatch on the popular initiative ‘Safeguarding Swiss Neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)’ (de)

Parliamentary debate 24.092 ‘Safeguarding Swiss neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)’, popular initiative (Curia Vista)

FAQ

Sanctions

  • Where sanctions are decided by the UN, as a member State Switzerland is bound to adopt them.

    The Embargo Act provides the legal foundation for adopting sanctions outside the UN. On this basis, the Federal Council decides on a case-by-case basis whether adopting the sanctions is in Switzerland’s interests. It may adopt sanctions imposed by the EU, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) or Switzerland’s main trading partners in full, in part or in an amended form. Following Russia’s illegal attack on Ukraine, the Federal Council decided to adopt most of the EU’s sanctions against Russia.

    When adopting sanctions Switzerland’s neutrality is relevant only if those sanctions concern goods that directly affect the military strength of a warring party. These are referred to as ‘militarily relevant goods’. If Switzerland restricts the export or transit of such goods for one warring party, it must apply the same restrictions to the other warring party, as required by the law of neutrality.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Sanctions

      PDF103.79 kB8 July 2026

  • States may respond with sanctions if other states violate international law. Recent years have seen an increase in sanctions imposed outside the UN framework. One of the reasons is that major powers are often unable to agree, so the UN Security Council sometimes cannot reach a decision. Outside the UN, states or regional organisations such as the EU may decide to impose sanctions. For example, the EU imposed sanctions against Russia in response to the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine. Even if they were not decided by the UN, adopting such sanctions is consistent with Switzerland’s neutrality.

    When Switzerland joins broadly supported sanctions – particularly in the event of a war of aggression against another State – its actions help to strengthen peace and a just international order. That is in Switzerland's own interest.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Sanctions

      PDF103.79 kB8 July 2026

Good offices

  • Good offices can help to de-escalate or resolve conflicts between states or within an individual state. In some cases they also serve to maintain dialogue between conflict parties, and to mitigate the consequences of armed conflict.

    Switzerland has a long tradition of good offices, and they are an important component of its foreign policy. They represent values that are associated with the state, such as reliability, discretion, rigour and impartiality.

    Neutrality is not a precondition for the ability to mediate credibly. However, alongside a Swiss political system built on dialogue, a willingness to compromise and cultural diversity, and characteristics such as discretion, expertise and flexibility, neutrality can reinforce trust in Switzerland and improve its credibility as a mediator.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Good Offices

      PDF113.18 kB8 July 2026

Exports of war materiel

  • Under the law of neutrality Switzerland is prohibited from supplying any material relevant for war purposes directly to parties to conflict from its own military inventory. In the case of private-sector exports Switzerland must treat all warring parties equally.  This means that if Switzerland restricts exports from private-sector entities to one party to a conflict, it must apply the same restrictions to the other party, as required by the principle of equal treatment.

    The War Materiel Act also applies. This goes beyond the law of neutrality. The War Materiel Act provides that export licences for war materiel will not be granted if the destination state is involved in international or non-international armed conflict. It applies equally to military inventory and private-sector entities.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and the export of war material

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026

  • The Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA) authorises overflights by foreign military and other state aircraft. Requests of major political importance, especially those concerning permits for flights relating to preparations or support for hostilities, are referred by the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC) to the Federal Council for decision. The Ordinance on the Protection of Airspace Sovereignty is the authoritative basis here.

    Decisions on arms exports must be made in accordance with the relevant legal foundations, specifically the Federal Act on War Materiel and the Goods Control Act. Here, too, the Federal Council decides on requests of major foreign or security policy importance.

    Neutrality is always taken into account when a decision is made.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and the export of war material

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026

  • Neutrality may for example also be a factor in the export of so-called as dual-use goods (i.e. those that can be used for both civilian and military purposes) and specific military goods (designed specifically for military purposes, but not classified as weapons or ammunition themselves; e.g. body armour). Their export to a country at war might also constitute the grant of military advantage, so the neutrality plays a role here too.

    Neutrality may also be of relevance in connection with private security services provided abroad. These services which fall under the Federal Act on Private Security Services Provided Abroad must be reviewed to ensure their consistency with neutrality. The services must be prohibited if they provide a militarily advantage to one party to a conflict.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and the export of war material

      PDF152.83 kB16 July 2026

Neutrality and security policy

  • Switzerland is subject to cross-border threats in just the same way as other European states. The security policy climate has become more uncertain and will remain unstable in the future. It is therefore in Switzerland's interest to align its security and defence policy with international cooperation.

    As a neutral state Switzerland is permitted to take part in international military exercises of a war context. Participation in such exercises does not come with any obligations of joint defence. These exercises allow Switzerland to enhance its own capabilities in comparison with foreign armed forces. If Switzerland were attacked, it would be able to cooperate with other states to defend itself. However, such cooperation cannot be practiced for only in an emergency, but must rather be trained for in advance.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality and Security Policy

      PDF141.89 kB8 July 2026

Switzerland’s neutrality

  • When the first Federal Constitution was drafted in 1848, neutrality was referred to in the provisions on the duties and powers of the Federal Assembly and the Federal Council.  The Federal Constitution states that the Federal Council and the Federal Assembly shall take ‘measures to safeguard […] Switzerland’s neutrality’ (Art. 173(1) and Art. 185(1) of the Federal Constitution).

    • Factsheet: Neutrality in the Federal Constitution

      PDF108.93 kB8 July 2026

  • As a permanently neutral state Switzerland does not participate under any circumstances in a war between states. It does not start any war, neither does it let itself become involved in any war. Permanent neutrality is first and foremost a commitment to peace.

    Armed neutrality means that Switzerland is able and ready to defend its territory. It can therefore also prevent its territory being misused for war-related purposes. This contributes to the credibility and effectiveness of Swiss neutrality.

  • The law of neutrality applies to armed conflict between states of a certain duration and intensity. The conflict is then referred to as a war in the sense of the law of neutrality, or as a neutrality case. The law of neutrality does not apply where the UN Security Council has passed a resolution that authorises military action.

    • Factsheet: law of neutrality, neutrality policy and neutrality in practice

      PDF159.57 kB16 July 2026

  • The decision on whether or not a neutrality case has arisen rests with the Federal Council. This is not usually an abstract decision, but one made in response to a specific need, such as overflights requests or adoption of sanctions.

    The application is made by the specialist government department concerned, for example:

    • the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research (EAER) in the case of sanctions and war materiel exports; or
    • the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC) in the case of overflights.
    • The Directorate of International Law (DIL) conducts the legal analysis in each case and is in constant contact with the competent authorities.

  • Applying the law of neutrality gives rise to the following obligations in relation to the parties to the conflict:

    • No transit of troops and weapons through Swiss territory or airspace;
    • A ban on exports of militarily relevant goods from Switzerland's own government inventory;
    • The duty to observe the principle of equal treatment in the case of private-sector exports of militarily relevant goods. ‘Militarily relevant’ refers to goods that directly support the combat capability of parties to a specific conflict in a militarily meaningful way.

    • Factsheet: law of neutrality, neutrality policy and neutrality in practice

      PDF159.57 kB16 July 2026

  • Neutrality is a substantial instrument of Swiss security, foreign and economic policy. It helps to safeguard Switzerland's interests and values in these areas.

    At the same time, neutrality has importance for domestic policy. Many people see it as a major element of the Swiss identity. That is why decisions on applying neutrality must take domestic policy factors into account in addition to foreign policy ones.

    In particular, neutrality supports the following interests and values that are embedded in the Federal Constitution:

    • independence and security
    • shared well-being
    • a just and peaceful international order.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality as an instrument

      PDF169.62 kB16 July 2026

  • Law of neutrality:

    The law of neutrality is part of international law. It governs how a neutral state must conduct itself towards belligerent states. Specifically, a neutral state may not:

    • take part in armed conflict between other states
    • provide military support to warring states
    • allow warring parties to use its territory.

    Within these rules of international law there is a degree of flexibility in how neutrality is applied.

    The law of neutrality becomes effective only in international conflicts of a certain duration and intensity.

    Neutrality policy:

    Neutrality policy covers policy decisions and measures that Switzerland takes to ensure that neutrality remains effective and credible, so that it is respected by other states.

    Neutrality in practice:

    The Federal Council and Parliament have employed neutrality to protect Switzerland's foreign, security and economic political interests ever since the federal state was established in 1848. This practice of neutrality abides by international law and grants the country the flexibility it needs to safeguard those interests in a range of foreign policy contexts. The Federal Council has set out its practice in numerous reports (see reports on the Iraq conflict and the conflict in Kosovo).

    Links

    Report on Swiss foreign policy in the 1990s (1993) (de)

    Neutrality under scrutiny in the Iran conflict (2005)

    Report on neutrality practice in Kosovo (2000)

    Clarity and guidance on neutrality policy – Federal Council report (2022)

    • Factsheet: law of neutrality, neutrality policy and neutrality in practice

      PDF159.57 kB16 July 2026

  • Switzerland needs a strong defence industry to defend itself. It is also dependent on key export markets. Trust in the reliability of Swiss defence companies would also be undermined if Switzerland ceased to be seen as a trustworthy security policy partner because it cooperated with its partners for the sole purpose of defending itself against attack.

    • Factsheet: Neutrality in the Federal Constitution

      PDF108.93 kB8 July 2026

    • Factsheet: law of neutrality, neutrality policy and neutrality in practice

      PDF159.57 kB16 July 2026

    • Factsheet: Neutrality as an instrument

      PDF169.62 kB16 July 2026

Other neutrality topics

  • There are other neutral states in addition to Switzerland. Each of them decides for itself what neutrality means in its particular case. This is why the practice of neutrality can differ widely.

    • Some states pursue permanent neutrality, such as Austria, Ireland and Costa Rica.
    • Other states invoke neutrality only in certain situations.

    Switzerland takes a special interest in the practices of the other European countries.

    • Factsheet: The neutrality of other countries

      PDF106.37 kB8 July 2026

  • Neutrality has never been a rigid concept, neither is it today. The way in which it is applied in practice is both by international law, as well as by the particular political and security policy circumstances of the time.

    The Federal Council's practice demonstrates that it has always used its room for manoeuvre in applying neutrality in the best interests of Switzerland.

    • Factsheet: A historical perspective on neutrality

      PDF230.15 kB17 July 2026

Index

Links

  • Convention concerning the Rights and Duties of Neutral Powers in Case of War at Sea (de, fr, it)
  • Convention concerning the Rights and Duties of Powers and Neutral Persons in Case of War on Land (de, fr, it)

Documents

  • Brochure: Swiss neutrality

    PDF546.64 kB3 March 2022

  • Clarity and direction in neutrality policy – Report of the Federal Council

    PDF1.25 MB26 October 2022

  • Report on neutrality practice in Kosovo

    PDF105.01 kB30 August 2000

  • Switzerland’s neutrality practice during the Iraq conflict

    PDF109.42 kB2 December 2005

  • White paper on neutrality 1993

    PDF120.71 kB29 November 1993

item.title: From Maputo to the mountain
item.description:
This book details the journey of the Maputo Accord. Written by Mirko Manzoni and Neha Sanghrajka, who supported and facilitated the mediation and negotiation of the Accord, it traces step-by-step the painstaking efforts to build trust and confidence in often challenging circumstances, drawing on the authors’ own recollections of the mediation and subsequent efforts to implement the Accord. Insights from the mediators and others closely associated with the process bring to life Mozambique’s unique journey towards peace and reconciliation and the courage, perseverance and innovation of everyone involved.

Mirko Manzoni, Neha Sanghrajka

Download View online version

Reviews:

“The Maputo Accord stands as a beacon of hope, not only for Mozambique but for the entire region, reminding us of the profound power of dialogue and diplomacy in building lasting peace. Switzerland is honored to have been a steadfast partner to Mozambique on this transformative journey, and we hope that this legacy of collaboration will inspire others in their own efforts to build a sustainable and peaceful future. Our continued support reflects Switzerland’s commitment to fostering enduring peace and shared prosperity in Mozambique, grounded in trust and partnership.”
IGNAZIO CASSIS, Federal Councillor, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Swiss Confederation

“I have been honoured to play a role in the peace process in Mozambique. Working closely with Neha and Mirko I vividly recall those initial tense conversations as we sought to help build the foundations of the peace process. Over the past number of years I have continued to follow progress as the process stands out for me as uniquely innovative and collaborative. It brought together diverse perspectives and succeeded in fostering mutual understanding and reconciliation, through dialogue and trust-building. The firsthand account shared in this book captures the complexities of peacemaking, unpacking the delicate negotiations, power dynamics and challenges of building lasting peace in Mozambique. Having been engaged in the process on the ground, I am delighted to read the full account, told in a balanced and thoughtful way. I firmly believe the lessons from Mozambique’s peace process provide valuable contributions to the fields of conflict resolution and modern mediation, offering relevant and timely insights for other contexts.”
JONATHAN POWELL, National Security Adviser of the United Kingdom

“I have witnessed meaningful progress in Mozambique’s peace efforts and commend the ongoing commitment to dialogue as a key tool for sustaining peace and advancing national reconciliation. Mozambique’s experience offers a compelling example of how African solutions can address African challenges and create sustainable pathways to peace. This way Silencing the Guns becomes more than an aspiration but a necessity for a prosperous Mozambique.”
DR. MOHAMED IBN CHAMBAS, African Union High Representative for Silencing the Guns

item.title: COP30: UN Climate Change Conference in Belém, Brazil Dossier The 30th UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) took place in Belém, Brazil, from November 10 to 21, 2025. This dossier compiles analyses and background information on key debates at COP30
item.description:
COP30 has shown that consensus in climate multilateralism is hard to find these days – with or without the US, which was absent for the first time. Key issues such as phasing out fossil fuels and delivering comprehensive climate finance to the Global South remain unresolved.

No agreement could be reached on a formal roadmap process for ending fossil fuels and deforestation. Instead, the Brazilian COP presidency announced that it would launch a roadmap process outside the official negotiations. Showing true leadership, Colombia is also committed to moving ahead: it has announced plans to organise the first global conference on phasing out fossil fuels in April 2026.

This shows once again the urgent need for reforms of the UNFCCC system to push the fossil fuel industry out of climate negotiations and enable effective multilateral decision-making and action – if needed against the interests of individual blocking governments that fight to uphold the status quo.

Finally, after a dragging struggle between Australia and Turkey on the hosting of COP31, a compromise was reached: Turkey will physically host COP31 in Antalya, but Australia will be lead on the political negotiations and will convene a pre-COP meeting in the Pacific.

item.title: آفاق تجدید العقد الاجتماعي في لبنان
item.description:
واجه لبنان سلسلة من الأزمات المتداخلة، بما في ذلك الانهيار المالي عام 2019، وانفجار مرفأ بيروت، والشلل المؤسسي، والاعتداءات الإسرائيلية المتكررة، وعدم الاستقرار السياسي والإقليمي المستمر، والتي أعادت تشكيل العلاقات بين الدولة والمواطنين بشكل جذري، وزادت من حدة تحديات الحوكمة المزمنة. في هذا السياق، أجرت مؤسسة وستمنستر للديمقراطية ومؤسسة بيرغوف بحثًا خلال الفترة من مارس إلى ديسمبر 2025 لدراسة كيفية فهم فئات متنوعة من المواطنين اللبنانيين للعقد الاجتماعي الحالي، وأولوياتهم لعقد متجدد وشامل، والعوائق والفرص المتاحة لتحقيقه.

Lara Azzam, Mohammad Al Mishlawi, Jana Sleem

item.title: Perspectives for a renewed social contract in Lebanon
item.description:
Lebanon has faced a succession of overlapping crises—including the 2019 financial collapse, the Beirut port explosion, institutional paralysis, recurring Israeli aggressions, and ongoing political and regional instability—that have profoundly reshaped state–citizen relations and intensified long-standing governance challenges. Against this backdrop, Westminster Foundation for Democracy, and the Berghof Foundation conducted research from March–December 2025 to examine how diverse groups of Lebanese citizens understand the current social contract, their priorities for a renewed and inclusive one, and the barriers and opportunities for achieving it.

Lara Azzam, Mohammad Al Mishlawi, Jana Sleem

item.title: It’s Time to Abandon Defensive Politics! Presidents' column Since Germany’s last federal election in 2025, its centrist parties have lost large numbers of voters to the fringes – particularly to the Right. At the same time, the Greens have also regained ground. A new study gives clues as to how a centre-left political platform can secure a strong governing majority. Jan Philipp Albrecht
item.description:
Zohran Mamdani in New York, Rob Jetten in the Netherlands, Sisse Marie Welling in Copenhagen, and Mark Carney in Canada have two main things in common: a proactive centre-left political agenda and recent success at the polls. But the similarities do not end there. The Heinrich Boell Foundation’s study "Wie Wahlen gewonnen werden" [How elections are won], published earlier this month, identifies recurring patterns in successful centre-left campaigns across different political contexts. While not claiming to provide a blueprint for electoral victory, the study does offer insights into which factors currently contribute most significantly to success. Four of these stand out in particular.

Leaders who connect with people

Successful election campaigns start with credible candidates. This does not mean that politicians must have universal appeal or represent every position. What is crucial is that people feel heard by a party’s senior figures and believe their concerns are being taken seriously. Such approachability must be genuine rather than orchestrated and backed by a party that also credibly embodies it.

Concrete proposals to improve people’s lives

It might sound clichéd, but particularly in the current geopolitical, economic, and social climate, concrete and feasible proposals for improving people’s lives must be at the forefront of political platforms. Affordable housing, free nursery places, reliable local transport – even being able to see trees from one’s window; these are tangible improvements that can be achieved through politics, in partnership with citizens. This is precisely where their political strength lies.

Denying the ”culture war” a foothold

The electoral successes of populist, authoritarian, right-wing forces have a common ingredient: exclusion, division, and polarisation. This dangerous mix has been particularly effective since at least the Covid-19 pandemic. Added to this is the spread of disinformation and hate on social media, including from abroad. Our study shows that by adopting a clear stance, an open tone, and an inclusive rather than divisive approach, the centre-left can achieve electoral success. Refusing to engage in identity politics – which, at its core, is designed to divide – and instead treating diverse backgrounds, thinking, and interests as democratic normality can take the wind out of populists’ sails.

The courage to embrace difference

Last but not least, the study demonstrates that there is no single, definitive approach that can guarantee success across all contexts. Globalisation and digitalisation mean that many political issues are now transnational. Yet people’s lives unfold not on a global scale but within families, neighbourhoods, local communities, and regions – under diverse structural, political, and cultural conditions and accompanied by a range of challenging situations. Successful campaigns take these differences seriously and develop proposals that are tailored to local situations.

While the study does not claim to provide a magic formula for electoral victory, it does reveal a recurring pattern in successful centre-left campaigns. Elections are not won by playing defensively or focusing on the issues raised by political opponents. They are won by those with a desire to shape the future and with their own clear, reality-based, workable proposals. Those on the centre-left who internalise this principle stand a good chance of regaining majorities. Cem Özdemir’s success in Baden-Württemberg demonstrates the potential inherent in this type of political platform. This provides the Greens in particular with the chance to learn the right lessons and counter defensive politics in this country. It is a matter of developing a political platform for Germany as a whole and assuming responsibility as a leader of the centre-left.

Get Involved - Presidents' column

Get involved! There’s no other way to be real – thus the message of Heinrich Böll, and, to this day, his encouragement is inspiring us. With this column the Presidents of the Foundation involve themselves in current social and political debates. This column will appear each month, authored, in turn, by Jan Philipp Albrecht and Imme Scholz.

item.title: ‘Has Your Family Seen This?’ Using Non-Sexual Images as Sexual Control in India Analysis What is lost, beyond their modesty, when non-sexual images of women and queer people are captured, circulated, or manipulated without their consent? Vandita Morarka, Karishma Shafi, Arshiya Kochar
item.description:
2nd January 2025, 10.00 AM: It’s the first morning of a New Year - new beginnings. A Kannada regional news channel is covering New Year’s celebrations in Bengaluru. The headlines read “Drunk young woman fights with police,” “Woman falls on the road and struggles” in an urgent yellow color against a black backdrop with thrilling music. Then the frame moves to women: drunk to varying degrees, wearing ‘revealing’ Western clothing. Sometimes they are being carried away by ‘responsible’ boyfriends or police personnel, other times they are screaming or fighting with guards, guests, or camerapersons.

 The same, unedited video of a drunk woman being carried by men to safety, with other generic clips of the crowd, has gone viral on platforms like X, Instagram and Facebook. The comment section reads “Destroyed by Western culture and some have problems with hijab and all”, “Girls are doing more drugs than boys, women empowerment is being taken full advantage of in the country”, and “Isko time pr parents ne treatment diya hota to ye haal nahi hota” (“If her parents had controlled her behavior earlier, this wouldn’t have happened”). 

Regardless of the geography or level of inebriation, the people captured and put on blast every year with such coverage have some things in common: they are mostly women, feminine-presenting, or queer; and they do not consent to it and do not anticipate being filmed and broadcast in a vulnerable state.

The objective of such media coverage, or indeed any coverage of such nature, is to use images to exercise social, moral, and sexual control on the bodies of its subjects and engineer a loss of dignity, autonomy, and privacy. In this way, an image need not necessarily constitute nudity, genital exposure, or sexual activity to cause harm. Understanding this underlying objective allows us to develop a more nuanced and culturally situated definition of image-based abuse. Crucially, it forces us to examine and expand on the different components of the traditional definition - do socio-cultural factors shape what counts as ‘intimate’ images? How does this impact the outcomes of the sharing of intimate images, including on people’s safety and well-being? 

Image-based sexual abuse (IBSA) refers to the creation (by capturing or manipulation), threat, or disclosure of intimate images of individuals to third parties without their consent.

Below, I present an Indian perspective on the use of non-explicit, non-consensual images to exercise sexual control and coercion on women’s and queer people’s bodies. I explore the role of AI technology in such abuse. Finally, I make the case for a more nuanced articulation of what ‘counts’ as image-based sexual abuse (IBSA) in India’s socio-cultural and legal context. 

‘Expanding’ IBSA: An Indian Perspective

Across India, women, assigned female at birth (AFAB), and femme-presenting people are excessively controlled from a young age to prevent, monitor, and control sexual activity and agency to prevent exogamy and pregnancy outside of caste-endogamous and externally-mediated marriage. This control is exerted in various social institutions like religion, education, and family by enforcing a complex and varying socio-cultural standard of modesty or propriety in behavior and presentation. Over time, this form of control becomes normalized under the guise of safety and care. Any behaviors or activities that do not adhere to this standard are then associated with deep personal, public, and generational shame. 

Against this context, women and queer people are forced to carve out spaces for themselves outside the purview of immediate family or community, where they can openly express their gender identity, gender expression or sometimes even consume alcohol, tobacco or drugs and dancing, i.e., activities that are culturally considered ‘shameful’. In this way, these activities become deeply personal or ‘intimate’. Thus, based on the socio-cultural norms they are bound by, the same image (like one taken during a meal or while lying down) may be intimate for one person and not so for another. Accordingly, while an act may not be sexual in nature, it may still qualify as intimate, and images of women, girls, and queer folks engaged in it may attract reputational damage for individuals and families.

Women and queer people are forced to carve out spaces for themselves, where they can openly express their gender identity.

This is especially true when images are used for coercion or manipulation, or to defame or ‘out’ a queer person. Punitive consequences imposed by family or community elders often follow, such as restricted mobility, restricted phone or internet use, forced marriage with the intent to ‘convert’ queer people, forced withdrawal from school, work, or social circles, emotional neglect or abuse, and (sometimes fatal) physical violence. By tightening the regulation of women’s and queer people’s sexualized bodies and limiting their bodily autonomy, harm is perpetrated using the same logic of sexual control as in IBSA, using images that are not sexual in nature. 

What Can Such Images Look Like, and How Are They Captured?

A phenomenon of particular note is the retroactive sexualization of photos and videos captured in public without consent, such as through discrete phone cameras, sensationalized mass media coverage, the use of Meta Glasses, or using Grok to undress or expose adults and children.

The proliferation of tech-facilitated image manipulation and circulation methods poses a unique risk for image-based abuse in the Indian context. First, it is becoming increasingly easier to generate or manipulate hyper-realistic deep-fake images that can be used to misattribute sexual and other activities to individuals without consent. Secondly, there is an increased uptake of digital social media like WhatsApp, and Facebook among the middle-aged and older Indian demographic, which is largely responsible for decision-making in families and communities. Finally, despite a nation-wide push for increased internet and mobile usage (including for digital banking and many bureaucratic processes), there are structural challenges like limited media literacy, as well as platform-specific hurdles like the inability to trace origins of ‘forwarded’ messages on WhatsApp or flag AI content on Facebook.

Unfortunately, the socio-cultural and functional nuances of the scope of IBSA are flattened by traditional legal definitions, which are non-comprehensive in the face of the fast-evolving nature of harm and means of perpetration. 

Recognizing a Loss of Autonomy Over Modesty

Traditionally, legislation in India around image-based abuse primarily deals with images that are directly sexual in nature. It uses the logic that such abuse outrages the modesty of women. Thus, it is primarily concerned with the contents of images - complete or partial nudity, genital exposure, or engagement in a sexual or ‘private’ act like using the lavatory; and the prevention of circulation and representation of such images. Accordingly, the broad legal framework is based on colonial-era notions of preserving women’s modesty, anti-voyeurism, and anti-obscenity1 rather than the violation of consent and privacy. 

Although legal recourse may be sought against the creation, modification, or circulation of non-consensual, non-sexual images through laws around defamation, criminal intimidation, or stalking, these provisions do not capture the nuances of how images can be used to cause gendered harm. However, a judicial foundation of a right-to-privacy-based approach does exist, with judgments like R. Rajagopal vs. State of Tamil Nadu (1994) and Justice K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India (2017) providing constitutional anchors for the right to privacy and one’s own name and likeness. More recently, the Madurai Branch of India’s Madras High Court noted that morphed images (such as with AI) are a ‘calculated assault on privacy, reputation, and emotional security’.

To apply a sensitive definition of image-based sexual abuse, we must challenge socio-cultural norms around gendered modesty, consent, intimacy, privacy and well-being.

Yet, this ad-hoc response and the limitations in how IBSA is institutionally defined push us to ask if an inclusive definition is possible. Importantly, such a definition would address the gendered nature of image-based harm in terms of social and sexual control and classify it based on intent as a violation of consent, privacy, and autonomy rather than an outrage of modesty. A definition of such scope would also move beyond purely sexually explicit images to account for retroactive sexualization and circulation of non-sexual, culturally-defined ‘intimate’ images to exert sexual control. It would also be useful for such articulation to acknowledge that the harm caused to women and queer people by image-based abuse is often a result of harmful internalized standards of modesty, inherited in legislation and social organization from a shared history of colonialization and, in some countries, patriarchal caste structures that predate colonialism. 

To pick apart, reframe, and meaningfully apply a more contextually sensitive definition of image-based sexual abuse is an exercise that invites us to challenge socio-cultural norms around gendered modesty, consent, intimacy, privacy, and well-being and expand the way we understand, define, and address gender-based violence. 

  • 1

    The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 20211 [updated as on 10.02.2026]

    Section 67 in The Information Technology Act, 2000

By tightening the regulation of women’s and queer people’s sexualized bodies and limiting their bodily autonomy, harm is perpetrated using the same logic of sexual control as in IBSA, using images that are not sexual in nature. 

What Can Such Images Look Like, and How Are They Captured?

A phenomenon of particular note is the retroactive sexualization of photos and videos captured in public without consent, such as through discrete phone cameras, sensationalized mass media coverage, the use of Meta Glasses, or using Grok to undress or expose adults and children.

The proliferation of tech-facilitated image manipulation and circulation methods poses a unique risk for image-based abuse in the Indian context. First, it is becoming increasingly easier to generate or manipulate hyper-realistic deep-fake images that can be used to misattribute sexual and other activities to individuals without consent. Secondly, there is an increased uptake of digital social media like WhatsApp, and Facebook among the middle-aged and older Indian demographic, which is largely responsible for decision-making in families and communities. Finally, despite a nation-wide push for increased internet and mobile usage (including for digital banking and many bureaucratic processes), there are structural challenges like limited media literacy, as well as platform-specific hurdles like the inability to trace origins of ‘forwarded’ messages on WhatsApp or flag AI content on Facebook.

Unfortunately, the socio-cultural and functional nuances of the scope of IBSA are flattened by traditional legal definitions, which are non-comprehensive in the face of the fast-evolving nature of harm and means of perpetration. 

Recognizing a Loss of Autonomy Over Modesty

Traditionally, legislation in India around image-based abuse primarily deals with images that are directly sexual in nature. It uses the logic that such abuse outrages the modesty of women. Thus, it is primarily concerned with the contents of images - complete or partial nudity, genital exposure, or engagement in a sexual or ‘private’ act like using the lavatory; and the prevention of circulation and representation of such images. Accordingly, the broad legal framework is based on colonial-era notions of preserving women’s modesty, anti-voyeurism, and anti-obscenity1 rather than the violation of consent and privacy. 

Although legal recourse may be sought against the creation, modification, or circulation of non-consensual, non-sexual images through laws around defamation, criminal intimidation, or stalking, these provisions do not capture the nuances of how images can be used to cause gendered harm. However, a judicial foundation of a right-to-privacy-based approach does exist, with judgments like R. Rajagopal vs. State of Tamil Nadu (1994) and Justice K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India (2017) providing constitutional anchors for the right to privacy and one’s own name and likeness. More recently, the Madurai Branch of India’s Madras High Court noted that morphed images (such as with AI) are a ‘calculated assault on privacy, reputation, and emotional security’.

To apply a sensitive definition of image-based sexual abuse, we must challenge socio-cultural norms around gendered modesty, consent, intimacy, privacy and well-being.

Yet, this ad-hoc response and the limitations in how IBSA is institutionally defined push us to ask if an inclusive definition is possible. Importantly, such a definition would address the gendered nature of image-based harm in terms of social and sexual control and classify it based on intent as a violation of consent, privacy, and autonomy rather than an outrage of modesty. A definition of such scope would also move beyond purely sexually explicit images to account for retroactive sexualization and circulation of non-sexual, culturally-defined ‘intimate’ images to exert sexual control. It would also be useful for such articulation to acknowledge that the harm caused to women and queer people by image-based abuse is often a result of harmful internalized standards of modesty, inherited in legislation and social organization from a shared history of colonialization and, in some countries, patriarchal caste structures that predate colonialism. 

To pick apart, reframe, and meaningfully apply a more contextually sensitive definition of image-based sexual abuse is an exercise that invites us to challenge socio-cultural norms around gendered modesty, consent, intimacy, privacy, and well-being and expand the way we understand, define, and address gender-based violence. 

  • 1

    The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 20211 [updated as on 10.02.2026]

    Section 67 in The Information Technology Act, 2000

item.title: The Orange Grove That Stopped Blooming Scrollytelling Tunisia is one of the most water-scarce countries in the world. Activists are fighting against political silence and calling for greater ecological awareness. Hannah El-Hitami
item.description:
When Rawè Kefi was born, her parents named her after a very special phenomenon. In Tunisia, Rawè is the name given to the first rain after a long drought. Rawè Kefi's father runs an orange farm in Menzel Bouzelfa in north-eastern Tunisia. Rawè Kefi remembers how when she was little, he and the other farmers would call each other as soon as the long-awaited rain arrived in December. "May the first rain bless you," they said, giving each other sweets and celebrating together. 

"I remember those days in winter when it rained and everybody was happy," says Rawè Kefi. "The orange grove was so green and vast, the colors so vivid. It was beautiful."

Today, Rawè Kefi is 29 years old and rarely visits her family's farm. "It is too painful to see the trees dying, one after the other." 

Some of the orange trees are as old as she is; she grew up with them. Now many of them are sick, their leaves brown and shriveled. 

Her family's farm is just one of many affected. Menzel Bouzelfa is known as the "orange capital." Tunisia's best oranges come from there, Rawè Kefi says proudly. But for years now, there has not been enough rain, and the soil is becoming salinated. Her father is now considering selling his farm. "For me, climate change is already a reality. It is palpable because I am experiencing it with my own family."

Tunisia Is One of the Most Water-Scarce Countries in the World

Rawè Kefi has spent half her life campaigning for protection of water and the environment – in a country that is one of the most water-scarce in the world. While each person in Germany consumes around 2,600 cubic meters of water per year, the people of Tunisia have only around 420 cubic meters per capita at their disposal.

The already scarce water resources are increasingly threatened by the climate crisis. Since 2017, there have been more frequent droughts with serious consequences for water and food security. Since President Kais Saied took power in 2019, he has isolated the country leading it into an economic crisis that leaves little room for modernizing agriculture or adapting to climate change. "People need to hear that we are in a state of national emergency," says Rawè Kefi. She wants to raise public awareness of the water crisis among Tunisians. She believes that each and every one should feel responsible – and that every individual can make a difference.

Rawè Kefi learned to save water early on, not only because she is the daughter of a farmer.

"My mother set up a system in our house for recycling domestic water. We believe that water is something very precious, a blessing from God that should not be wasted." 

The water the family uses for showering is later used to flush the toilet, and wastewater from the kitchen is used to water the plants. 

“We always had the cheapest water bill in the whole neighborhood, if not the whole city”, Rawè Kefi says laughing.

Listening to Rawè Kefi, it's hard not to feel hopeful. She talks fast but in a structured way, smiles a lot and gestures energetically. She has just submitted her doctoral thesis, which deals with art and culture in the context of nature and climate. She recently began teaching environmental humanities at a university in Tunis. This new interdisciplinary research field uses social science perspectives to rethink environmental issues.

Raising Awareness Through Art

"I believe in the power of art and culture to move people’s consciences," says Rawè Kefi, who has herself experimented with environmental poetry. "If I just present people with facts and diagrams, I will not interest them in environmental issues. But if I use poetry slams, music or poetry, I can reach them on a different level." Among other things, Kefi led a project with schoolchildren to create plays, rap songs and short films on the topic of water conservation.

Her work often focuses on the younger generation. Rawè Kefi is committed to ensuring that young people learn about environmental protection at an early age – not only through theoretical lessons in school, but by experiencing nature for themselves. 

As a member of the Tunisian organization "Réseau Enfants de la Terre" (Network of the Children of the Earth), she currently mentors 240 young activists between the ages of 8 and 30 who are researching the effects of climate change in all 24 governorates of Tunisia.

Addressing the Tunisian Government

She is also a member of the Tunisian Young Climate Change Negotiators. The initiative was founded in 2021 by the Tunisian Ministry of Environment and was the first of its kind in West Asia and North Africa. In order to involve young people in decisions on climate change, participants learn how climate policy works and how it is negotiated at the international level. Once a year, they accompany the Tunisian delegation to international climate summits.

Rawè Kefi’s experience as a climate negotiator is evident: she has a clear vision of her demands to the Tunisian government and its political and economic partners. On the one hand, she is concerned with the economic dimension: "Despite the crisis we are living in, the government is still exporting goods with a high water footprint, like oranges, dates, strawberries or watermelons." Like many countries in the Global South, Tunisia is heavily indebted and dependent on foreign currency. Focusing on the export economy is a way of dealing with this situation, but " the amount of water we are losing cannot be repaid with foreign currency," believes Rawè Kefi. In her view, trade agreements, especially with the EU, need to be reviewed urgently.

From a legal perspective, she calls for stricter sanctions against water wastage, especially by national and international private companies. Overuse and pollution of water should be punished as "ecocide", she says. "I am not against the private sector, but it has a social and environmental responsibility. It has to find ways to repair the damage it causes."

Water Diplomacy Instead of Conflict With Neighboring Countries

In addition, Rawè Kefi expects the Tunisian government to focus more on water diplomacy – to avoid political conflicts over transboundary waters with neighboring countries in the future. Instead, the goal should be greater cooperation. Above all she wants the government to raise awareness of the water crisis. "The government should stop reassuring people. Everyone needs to understand that this is an emergency – as if a war had broken out."

Every single person should feel responsible for solving the water crisis. 

"I don't want to individualize the crimes. The government holds the most responsibility. 

But I truly believe that we as individuals can make a contribution, no matter how small, in our households, our neighborhoods, our schools." 

Water in Tunisia

  • In outdated pipe networks, nearly 30 percent of tap water seeps away.
  • An estimated 300,000 people do not have regular access to drinking water.
  • Protests over water shortages have become a defining feature of the country’s summer months – in 2024 alone, 186 protests were recorded.

Working together with others, taking action instead of just being afraid, gives Rawè Kefi hope despite the worsening water crisis. Through this commitment, she has developed a deeper connection to her country, which she calls "ecological citizenship". 

"I love my country for its nature and ecosystems. With this sense of belonging, we can make our Tunisia green again."

item.title: Agroecology in Italy: Farming the Future Analysis For rural communities and the farming sector, saving water and energy is a key pillar of adaptation to climate change. Agroecology goes beyond the limits of organic farming by linking agricultural, environmental, social and economic choices into a unified system. Margherita Ambrogetti Damiani, Angelo Gentili, Carlotta Priore, Legambiente Agricoltura
item.description:
In an era marked by the increasingly obvious effects of the climate crisis, water conservation is no longer about simply conforming to best practices. It is rather about survival and adaptation. Heatwaves, torrential rains and extreme drought are no longer exceptional events; they have become the new normal. From 2010 to 2025, Italy experienced hundreds of floods, river overflows and landslides caused by heavy rainfall. IPCC experts warn that the future will be characterized by increasingly intense swings between drought and violent downpours.1 

These are impacts that affect not only ecosystems, but also the economy, agriculture, and quality of life. Crops are shifting, yields are shrinking, animal and plant species are altering their lifecycles. In Sicily, Calabria and Puglia, exotic fruits have now partly replaced the traditional crops, while in Valle d’Aosta the vineyards are climbing the slopes in search of a milder climate. It’s a situation that demands urgent and systematic decisions regarding the management of natural resources, and the reduction of waste and inefficiencies in favour of a more resilient production model.

Water Management Is One of the Most Critical Issues

Conserving water means securing a future for the agriculture sector and rural communities. This is a challenge that demands shared strategies, adaptation plans and a culture of prevention. Managing climate risk relies on the ability to read the land, monitor impacts, and take action before any damage occurs. Every production chain should implement risk assessment and risk management plans based on up-to-date climate scenarios and early-warning systems.

One of the most critical issues is water management. On average, agricultural irrigation accounts for 50 percent of national water withdrawals2, with peaks in the areas with the most agriculture. Given the fluctuations in water availability, work is required on two fronts: reducing demand and increasing efficiency.

The situation demands urgent and systematic decisions regarding the management of natural resources.

Reducing demand means revising the farming model. In many areas it will be necessary to accelerate the transition toward less water-intensive crops, gradually abandoning crops that are no longer sustainable in a context of structural drought. Regional farming plans and guidelines should integrate up-to-date climate scenarios, and avoid investment that is incompatible with future water availability. Prevention also includes systematic action: collection and reuse of rainwater, reuse of process water, maintenance of hedges and plant borders that slow down runoff and reduce erosion.

In parallel, the efficiency of irrigation has to be improved. Drip irrigation, which is currently the most effective technique, is capable of over 90 percent efficiency, especially when coupled with moisture sensors, agrometeorological observatories and variable-rate irrigation systems (VRI). While these measures require planning and investment, they also improve resilience and water availability.

Techniques such as natural mulching also help to preserve soil moisture, reduce evaporation and protect plants from temperature swings. Today, this ancient practice has gained a newfound strategic importance. The gradual intensification of climate change has pushed many farmers to increase their use of pesticides and fertilizers. And yet less than five percent of the active ingredient reaches the target organism, leaving the rest to be dispersed into the environment, so contaminating water, air and soil. This is an approach that can make agricultural supply chains even more vulnerable.

Energy Saving Means Finding a Balance Between Innovation and Responsibility

Energy saving also involves walking a line between innovation and responsibility. Reducing consumption is not just an economic question, but an essential commitment to sustainability. Improving the efficiency of agricultural facilities and using less energy-intensive equipment as well as renewable sources – from solar power to heat pumps – are investments that pay back their cost over time. Maintenance, monitoring consumption, and optimizing the production process reduces waste and emissions, while also improving competitiveness. 

Technological innovation is a clear ally in this battle. Automated systems and smart sensors allow for the collection and analysis of data on water and energy consumption, which enables more precise management. Dedicated software enables the discovery of inefficiencies and leaks in real time, making sustainability a continuous and quantifiable process3. 

Nevertheless, no technology can take the place of collective wisdom. It is essential to foster a culture of conservation and respect for the environment in order to ensure that change is durable. By informing, training and involving farmers and communities, strategies can be transformed into concrete action. Every act, no matter how small, makes a difference. Repairing a leak, optimizing a facility, reducing energy consumption – it all contributes to ecological regeneration.

It is essential to foster a culture of conservation and respect for the environment in order to ensure that change is durable.

Good practices work. In many Italian and European agricultural businesses, integrated strategies of water conservation have produced tangible results: reduced costs, greater resilience against extreme weather, productivity growth, and a stronger reputation among consumers. Businesses that invest in sustainability reduce their impact and become laboratories of innovation and responsibility. 

Adopting a sustainable approach does not mean giving up on development, but rather changing the model: smarter, fairer, more respectful of the planet’s limits. Saving water and energy is both a technical decision and a vision of the future. And it’s a transition that has to begin today, in the fields, in businesses, in homes – wherever an everyday gesture can become care for the Earth. 

This article was first published in Italian by the Heinrich Böll Foundation's Office in Paris. It was translated by Ciaran Lawless, edited by Robin Gleeson.

  • 1

    Liverman, D. (2008). Assessing impacts, adaptation and vulnerability: Reflections on the Working Group II Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Global environmental change, 18(1), 4-7.

  • 2

    Sustainable Water Use in Agriculture within the Framework of the NRRP (The National Recovery and Resilience Plan).

  • 3

    Provera, I. Agricoltura 4.0: l’irrigazione efficace e sostenibile in pieno campo.
